notes: Training classes catalog, grouped by category (Fundamentals / Genre-specific / Advanced / Specialized). Each course: category, price 'free' (teaser ships with the app) or 'paid' (unlocked by redemption code / purchase), lessons with video_url (direct MP4 or YouTube/Vimeo link), and optional practice_preset — camera settings the lesson's 'Try it' button loads into the simulator (values snap to the selected camera). Post-processing lessons intentionally have no practice_preset: they teach editing, not camera settings. The free courses are the shipped teasers; sample video URLs are CC0 placeholders (MDN friday.mp4, has audio) — swap in your hosted lessons.

courses.title: Beginner Photography Class
courses.tagline: Know your camera before you touch a setting — the complete 11-lesson class
courses.description: A complete beginner class built around understanding the camera first, in eleven lessons: the parts and the light (1), camera types and choosing equipment (2), lenses and perspective (3), shooting modes (4), the exposure triangle (5), focus and autofocus (6), composition (7), lighting (8), white balance and color (9), putting it all together in an intentional everyday photo (10), and the workflow that protects your originals — import, organize, select, edit, export (11). Every lesson ends in the app's simulator, so you practice on real controls while you watch.

lessons.title: How a Camera Works
lessons.summary: A photograph begins with light: the lens gathers it, the aperture meters how much passes, the shutter times how long the sensor sees it, and the sensor records the image. Learn the visible parts, then follow the light through a DSLR — where a mirror feeds the optical viewfinder until the shot flips it away — and a mirrorless body, where the sensor itself drives the live view. Designs vary between models; following the light is the map that works on all of them.
lessons.practice_brief: Open the 📷 Camera body tab and tap through all six views: find the lens, the viewfinder or screen, and the shutter button on the DSLR — the pins explain each part's job. Then do it again on the Phone body and notice the same jobs live in different places. Finish by tracing the light out loud: lens → aperture → shutter → sensor, mirror for a DSLR's viewfinder, straight to the sensor on a mirrorless.

lessons.title: Camera Types and Choosing Equipment
lessons.summary: Start with what you want to photograph, not a brand name. Four camera types cover most beginners: a phone, a camera with a built-in lens, a DSLR, and a mirrorless body — each trading convenience against flexibility. Interchangeable-lens cameras add mounts: lenses must physically and electronically fit the body, and compatibility is checked per camera, lens, and adapter — never assumed.
lessons.practice_brief: Use the camera picker as your comparison table: switch between Phone, a Canon DSLR (Rebel SL3 — EF mount), and a Canon mirrorless (R50 — RF mount) and watch the Mounted-lens list change with the body. Only compatible lenses ever appear — that is the lesson. Then write down what you most want to photograph, what matters most (convenience, built-in zoom, changing lenses, direct controls), and the simplest setup that meets that need.

lessons.title: Lens Basics: Focal Length, Prime vs Zoom, and Perspective
lessons.summary: Focal length, marked in millimeters, governs how much of the scene fits in the frame — shorter includes more, longer shows a narrower view with the subject larger. A prime lens is one focal length; a zoom covers a range, and neither is automatically better. The other half of the story is where you stand: moving the camera changes perspective — how subject and background relate — and no amount of zooming undoes it. Compare focal lengths from the same position; move your feet for perspective.
lessons.practice_brief: Open the Mounted-lens selector and compare lenses on the same photo: a prime (Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 — one focal length, no range to turn) versus a zoom (EF-S 18-55) versus a long zoom (RF 100-400). The 🔍 LENS SWAP badge shows how much tighter each one frames versus your as-shot focal length — that is focal length changing framing from one fixed position. Perspective is the part the simulator can't do: it needs your feet. Take the same shot from two distances in the field and compare how the subject and background relate.

lessons.title: Shooting Modes and Camera Settings
lessons.summary: Shooting modes decide how much of the exposure process you hand over. Auto and Program (P) let the camera make most decisions; aperture-priority (Av or A) has you choose the aperture — your depth-of-field dial — while the camera picks a shutter speed; shutter-priority (Tv or S) is the reverse for controlling motion. Manual (M) gives you both dials, and ISO may be yours or Auto. Labels vary by brand — Canon says Av/Tv where Nikon and Sony say A/S — so learn your own camera's names, and remember the camera's choices have limits in dim light.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator puts you in M mode — every dial is yours. First walk all three dials one step each and say out loud which exposure variable each one drives. Then see 'the camera's' side: apply the coach's recommended settings and watch it land on a balanced combination — that's what a program does in a blink. In the field, pick aperture-priority (Av/A) or shutter-priority (Tv/S), change the scene's light without moving much, and note which setting you chose, which the camera adjusted, and whether your ISO is on Auto.

lessons.title: The Exposure Triangle
lessons.summary: Exposure is how bright or dark a photo looks, and three settings control it together. Aperture meters the light through the lens and shapes depth of field — wider (smaller f-number) brightens and blurs the background; narrower keeps more in focus. Shutter speed times the light and shapes motion — faster freezes, slower blurs. ISO sets the sensor's sensitivity — raising it brightens but invites noise. There is no universally 'right' setting: choose the look you want, then balance the other two dials around it.
lessons.practice_brief: Make three versions of the scene in front of you, changing one setting at a time — the simulator's live histogram makes each trade visible. 1) Open the aperture two stops: watch brightness rise AND background blur grow. 2) Speed the shutter two stops: brightness falls; motion effects you'll see in the field. 3) Raise ISO two stops: brightness rises and grain appears. After each, answer the lesson's question: what changed besides the number? When you're ready for the deep dive, the free 7-lesson Mastering the Exposure Triangle class is in your Classes list.

lessons.title: Focus and Autofocus Basics
lessons.summary: Focus placement is the choice of which part of the scene appears sharp — and it's separate from exposure: a perfectly exposed photo can still be sharp in the wrong place. Autofocus is a capable tool, but the photographer guides it onto the intended subject; modes and focus-area controls vary by model, so learn yours rather than mastering them all. And never trust the small screen: a photo that looks sharp in playback can reveal missed focus enlarged — review the important detail up close.
lessons.practice_brief: Open the aperture wider than your as-shot value first — that wakes up the ⊹ Focus point, since placement only matters when depth of field is thin. Drag the focus dot onto the subject's detail and watch sharpness bloom there; drag it to the background and watch the subject go soft. That is focus placement. In the field: guide autofocus onto a person's eye or an object's detail, take the photo, then zoom in on playback to check the DETAIL is sharp — if focus missed, place it more deliberately and shoot again.

lessons.title: Composition Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Composition is how elements are arranged in the frame — and every frame includes some things and leaves others out, which is what guides the viewer's attention. Three tools, options rather than rules: balance (a subject needn't be centered to feel settled), leading lines (paths, railings, rows of objects that walk the eye toward the subject), and the rule of thirds (placing important elements off-center near grid lines or intersections). Centered works too, when it suits the subject. The goal is an intentional choice, not a correct one.
lessons.practice_brief: In the field, make three photos of one subject: centered, off-center along a third (turn on your camera's grid display if it has one), and one using a leading line or natural frame like a doorway. Review all three and ask where your eye lands first. In the app, run the same photo through the coach with a style selected and read its composition notes, and use the lens selector to compare wider versus tighter framing of the same scene — framing is literally what gets included.

lessons.title: Lighting Basics: Direction, Softness, and Mood
lessons.summary: Light's direction and quality shape shadows, contrast and mood before any dial is touched. Front light flattens and flatters; side light sculpts — shape and texture show through stronger shadows; backlight rims the subject or silhouettes it, and often tricks the meter into darkening your subject. Softness follows the source's apparent size: bigger or diffused sources make gentle, gradual shadows; small hard sources make crisp edges and contrast. Moving the subject or yourself changes the light in the frame — and the exposure along with it.
lessons.practice_brief: In the field: one subject, three photos — front light, side light, backlight. For each, note where the light comes from, whether the shadow edges are soft or hard, and how the exposure looks. Backlight will try to silhouette your subject; that's the meter reacting to the bright background. In the app, see that reaction directly: use the EV buttons in the histogram guide to darken and brighten and watch the whole shape slide — a backlit frame leans bright while your subject sits dark, and −/EV or spot metering is the rescue. Move the subject or your feet and the light changes with you.

lessons.title: White Balance and Color
lessons.summary: Light sources have color: indoor bulbs lean warm, shade leans cool — and a color cast shifts every color in the frame. White balance is the camera's rendering control: it makes neutral objects — white paper, gray fabric — actually look neutral under the current light. Auto white balance does a decent job but interprets the scene its own way; presets and custom settings hand control back to you. Preset names and results vary by camera, so judge the image, not the label. And a cast isn't always a mistake — a deliberate warm or cool shift is a creative choice.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator renders white balance for real: keep everything else fixed and cycle the White balance setting — AWB, then Shade (which warms), then Tungsten (which cools to correct warm bulbs) — and watch the colors swing while brightness doesn't move. Judge like the lesson says: which version looks natural, and which makes a better deliberate mood? Then the field version: the same neutral-object subject near a window and again under indoor lights, AWB plus one preset each — note the light source, the setting, and what changed.

lessons.title: Taking Better Everyday Photos
lessons.summary: An intentional photo starts before the shutter: what do I want the viewer to notice? Notice the subject and the light's direction and quality, then choose a viewpoint, framing, focus point, and exposure that support it — changing viewpoint or framing often does more than touching settings. There is no required camera, mode, or gear: the aim is to make choices deliberately and understand their effects. Thoughtful decisions matter more than equipment.
lessons.practice_brief: The capstone drill uses your whole toolbox. Pick an ordinary subject — a cup, a plant, your desk. Photo 1: snap it without thinking. Photo 2: change at least two choices — move closer or lower, use side light, simplify the background, reframe, refocus, adjust exposure. Add both to the gallery and load each into the coach (🖼️ in the workspace) — compare the two responses; the score difference is your decision difference. Then replay either shot in the simulator: lens swaps for framing, the focus dot for placement, EV for exposure — before-and-after without re-shooting.

lessons.title: Basic Photo Organization and Editing
lessons.summary: The shot isn't finished when the shutter closes. Protect your originals — edit in a way that leaves them intact, or save edited versions as separate copies. Organize consistently (a folder per project or date; findable beats clever). Select with purpose: focus, expression, composition, light, and whether the photo says what you intended. Edit with a light touch — brightness, contrast, and color can lift a photo, while strong changes push it unnatural. The workflow — import, organize, select, edit, export — applies across every camera and program, even when the buttons don't.
lessons.practice_brief: Run the whole workflow in the app: pick a small set into your gallery (import), swipe away the misfires (organize), load your top three into the coach and use its scores and notes to choose favorites (select — say why, out loud). Then on the winner, preview a restrained edit: nudge exposure comp for brightness, try a picture style for contrast, shift white balance for color — the histogram keeps you honest, and the gallery original never changes. When it looks right, recreate those same small moves in your editing app and export a copy — original untouched.

courses.title: Intermediate Photography Class
courses.tagline: From knowing the dials to making them obey — the complete 13-lesson class
courses.description: The Beginner class built understanding; this class builds operational fluency, in thirteen lessons: manual exposure in practice (1), metering and exposure compensation (2), depth of field as a predictable four-factor system (3), motion and shutter speed as creative choice (4), advanced autofocus (5), composition beyond the basics (6), working with natural light (7), flash and reflectors (8), portrait photography (9), landscape and travel (10), RAW processing (11), color and black-and-white editing (12), and a consistent workflow that protects your originals (13). Every lesson ends in the app's simulator or a field drill with written observations.

lessons.title: Manual Exposure in Practice
lessons.summary: Manual mode is about consistency: when you choose the settings, the camera can't second-guess the look. Read the meter as a guide, not a command, and build exposures in decision order — the dial that drives the look first (aperture for blur, shutter for motion), the next dial for the light, and ISO to balance. Know the limits: in dim light every dial hits an end, and ISO takes the remainder.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator is all-manual — use it to drill the decision order twice on the same photo. Version A (portrait with blurred background): aperture first — open it wide for the look, then shutter, then ISO. Version B (moving subject kept sharp): shutter first — speed it up, then aperture, then ISO. Write down which dial led each version. In the field, photograph both situations for real in Manual and compare your decision notes.

lessons.title: Exposure Metering and Exposure Compensation
lessons.summary: The meter reads reflected light and aims every scene at middle brightness — which is wrong for genuinely bright and genuinely dark subjects. Snow turns gray; dark subjects turn hazy. Exposure compensation shifts the camera's recommendation in stops, brighter or darker, in automatic and semi-automatic modes. Learn where the control lives before you need it, and let the image or histogram referee every correction.
lessons.practice_brief: Open the histogram guide (click the histogram) and use its ±EV buttons: push the exposure brighter and darker and watch the whole tonal shape slide — that is exposure compensation, visible. Then the field drill: a light subject on a dark background and a dark subject on a light background, each shot at plain auto exposure and again with compensation both directions. Note the values you preferred. In full Manual there is nothing to compensate — the dials themselves are the adjustment.

lessons.title: Depth of Field
lessons.summary: Depth of field — the zone of acceptably sharp focus — responds to four factors, and aperture is only one. Wider apertures thin it; longer focal lengths thin it at the same framing; focusing closer shrinks it; and the background's distance behind the subject governs how visible the blur is. Predict the zone before you shoot, using all four factors, and let the photograph grade the prediction.
lessons.practice_brief: Predict, then check. Open the aperture wider than your as-shot value so depth of field activates, then say all four factors out loud and predict thin or deep before touching anything. Move the focus dot to re-place the zone, swap to a longer lens to thin it further, stop down to deepen. Subject distance and background distance aren't simulated — those two factors are field work: shoot the same subject close and far, with the background near and distant, and grade your predictions.

lessons.title: Motion and Shutter Speed
lessons.summary: Motion is a creative choice. Freezing depends on subject speed, direction, and distance — faster, crossing, and closer all demand more shutter. Slow shutters make motion the story: silk water, light ribbons, panning that keeps the subject recognizable inside streaks. And blur isn't always the subject's fault — camera shake smears the whole frame below your hand-holding floor, tamed by faster shutters, stabilization, or support. Choose the blur you want; fix the blur you don't.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator renders motion smear and camera shake honestly. Walk the shutter ladder down from 1/250 and watch the smear grow — that's subject motion becoming visible. Then mount an image-stabilized lens and repeat: the shake floor drops several stops, because stabilization tames YOUR movement, not the subject's. In the field: photograph a moving subject at two shutter speeds — one frozen, one showing motion on purpose — and one handheld frame below your shake floor to study what your own unsteadiness looks like.

lessons.title: Advanced Autofocus Techniques
lessons.summary: Autofocus is a partnership: the camera does the micro-adjustments, you decide what it locks onto. Single mode locks once for stationary subjects; continuous keeps chasing movement. Focus areas trade control for convenience — point, zone, or wide — and tracking plus subject detection are powerful but model-dependent. The review loop (shoot, enlarge, sort, adjust) is where the hit rate actually improves.
lessons.practice_brief: Set the focus mode control (AF-S vs AF-C on most brands) and photograph a moving person or object in continuous mode: choose a focus area, shoot a short series, review enlarged, and count sharp frames. Change ONE variable — area size, or single vs continuous — and shoot another series; compare hit rates. In the simulator, place the focus dot deliberately on the same detail every frame to build the placement reflex the review loop depends on.

lessons.title: Composition Beyond the Basics
lessons.summary: From rules to decisions. Visual weight: brightness, contrast, sharpness, color and faces pull the eye — arrange the weights deliberately so nothing out-pulls your subject by accident. Layers give a flat frame depth: near element, subject, far context. Negative space is emphasis — as long as it stays clean. Viewpoint is the free dial: move before you adjust anything else.
lessons.practice_brief: Photograph one subject three ways: built in layers (near element, subject, far context), small inside deliberately clean negative space, and using an unusual balance that still holds together. Review all three and name what pulls the eye first in each — if something out-pulls your subject, re-weigh or exclude it. In the app, the coach's composition notes give you a second opinion on placement.

lessons.title: Working with Natural Light
lessons.summary: From recognizing light to working it. Open shade is the flattering default — soft, even, with a sunlit boundary for depth. Backlight dramatizes — rim glow or silhouette, decided by where the exposure points — and fools the meter. Harsh sun squints and over-contrasts; four fixes in order of ease: shade, position, patience, purpose. Bounce from nearby surfaces is free fill. When the light changes, the exposure changes: move first, adjust second.
lessons.practice_brief: Photograph one subject under two different natural lights — open shade and backlight, or shade and sun. For each, note direction and softness, state what you changed to make it work (subject position, your position, or exposure), and choose which version suits the mood. In the app, use the histogram guide's EV buttons to see the meter's reaction you just lived through in the field.

lessons.title: Using Flash and Reflectors
lessons.summary: Light can be redirected or added. A reflector re-routes what already exists — white neutral, silver punchy, gold warm. A flash carries its own sun, and modern metering makes the basic workflow simple. Every added light answers to three levers: position shapes, distance changes brightness fast (the inverse-square rule), and size sets hardness. Ambient exposure owns the room; flash owns the subject. One lever at a time.
lessons.practice_brief: Field drill with one tool at a time: baseline portrait as found (heavy shadow side), then a reflector or white surface opposite the main light — closer, then farther — and finally flash if available, adjusting power or distance one step per frame. Write down which lever moved and what the light did. There's no flash simulation in the app — this lesson is honest field and equipment work.

lessons.title: Portrait Photography
lessons.summary: A strong portrait uses light, focus, composition, and exposure — but settings are the smallest part. Plan subject, location, and light first; direct the subject with actions rather than poses; focus the near eye and scan the frame edges before every shot. Saved recipes (the app's Portrait style carries one) start each session from experience instead of zero.
lessons.practice_brief: Load the Portrait style from the style selector — it carries a real recipe (wide-aperture priority) that starts your session from experience. Then the field series: a willing subject, open shade or window light, a background that helps. Give actions, not poses; focus the near eye; scan the edges. End by letting the subject pick their favorite frame — their answer teaches you something no histogram can.

lessons.title: Landscape and Travel Photography
lessons.summary: A place is many photographs. Light makes the appointment — scout it with maps and sun position. Collect three kinds of frame everywhere you go: the wide establishing view with a deliberate foreground anchor, the detail the wide frame would swallow, and the scale shot that lets the viewer feel the size. Work the viewpoint instead of taking one frame, and pack for the subject, not the anxiety.
lessons.practice_brief: Load the Landscape style for its recipe and priorities, then photograph a nearby place three ways: the wide establishing view with a foreground anchor, a detail the wide frame would have swallowed, and a scale shot with a person or bicycle against the scene. Review the three as a story — does it say what the place felt like? Note what you would shoot differently at a different hour.

lessons.title: Introduction to RAW Processing
lessons.summary: RAW is the ingredients; JPEG is a finished print the camera made for you. RAW files hold the sensor's nearly untouched readings, which is why they look flat, weigh more, and need software support verified per camera and editor. Edit in a restrained order — exposure, highlights and shadows, contrast, color — with small purposeful steps. The strongest edit is invisible, and the original file never changes.
lessons.practice_brief: Software does the editing — the app helps you choose WHAT deserves editing. Analyze a batch in the coach first: its scores and issues tell you which file has the most to give (the one with recoverable highlights, the nearly-sharp one). Edit that one in your RAW editor using the restrained order, then re-analyze the exported copy to see how far the file traveled. Reasons, not numbers, are the habit.

lessons.title: Color and Black-and-White Editing
lessons.summary: Color and black and white are two languages. Color speaks in relationships — warm against cool, complementary against clashing — edited with restraint rather than cranked saturation. Black and white is a translation, not a filter: hues collapse into tonal weight, texture rises, and separation must be earned by contrast. Choose the language that serves what the photograph is about, and say the purpose in one sentence.
lessons.practice_brief: Preview the translation in the simulator: switch the picture style to Monochrome and watch a color photo become a tonal one — does the subject still separate from the background? Choose a photo with a strong color element, make both versions (color adjusted for relationships; mono translated for tone), and write one sentence stating the purpose of each. No sentence, no deliberate choice yet.

lessons.title: Building a Consistent Editing Workflow
lessons.summary: Five stages — import, organize, select, edit, export — with backup riding over all of them. Consistency beats sophistication: findable beats clever. Leave cards untouched until copies are verified; mark favorites with reasons; keep originals sacred and exports separate; and keep a second copy somewhere else, automatic enough to actually happen. The library, not the shoebox.
lessons.practice_brief: The app is the first three stages. Import a small set into your gallery (pick photos), organize by swiping away the misfires, and select favorites by loading each into the coach and recording its score and top issue — reasons on record. The Progress screen becomes your archive habit. Edit the winner in your RAW editor and export a copy; back up originals and exports to a second location, then verify you can find both without searching twice.

courses.title: Advanced Photography Class
courses.tagline: Master the limits, find your voice — the complete 12-lesson class
courses.description: The capstone class, in twelve lessons: dynamic range as deliberate sacrifice (1), off-camera flash (2) and multi-light portraiture (3), composition as visual storytelling (4), the specialist genres and their priority orders (5), long exposure and night technique (6), panorama, focus stacking and HDR (7), color management and print preparation (8), advanced retouching (9), image selection and sequencing (10), developing a personal style (11), and ethics, permission and responsible photography (12). Every lesson ends in the simulator or a field drill with written observations.

lessons.title: Advanced Exposure and Dynamic Range
lessons.summary: High-contrast scenes exceed the sensor's span — and something gets lost. Choose what: shadows as graphic, highlights as look, added light to fit the span, or brackets to blend later. The histogram is the forecast: a shape touching both walls is the signal to pick a strategy before the shutter, not in the edit.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator's histogram guide emulates the strategies: push exposure up and down with the EV buttons and watch which wall the shape approaches — that is the dynamic-range forecast. Then the field drill: one high-contrast scene three ways (protect highlights, protect shadows, bracket two stops apart), writing down what each version sacrificed.

lessons.title: Off-Camera Flash and Lighting Setups
lessons.summary: Take the flash off the camera and the light's angle becomes a creative decision. Verify sync, choose a modifier for the shadow quality — size is softness — and learn positions by moving one light through its arc: 45 degrees models, 90 divides, behind rims. Key sets the look; fill softens what the key made. That habit scales to any studio.
lessons.practice_brief: No flash simulation in the app — this drill is honest field and equipment work. Build the one-light portrait: 45 degrees modified, then three positions, then fill from the opposite side. State position and power for every frame. Use the app's portrait style afterward as the baseline the lit version should beat.

lessons.title: Multiple-Light Portraiture
lessons.summary: Studio portraiture is one key light doing the main work, plus assistants with single jobs: fill opens the key's shadows, a rim separates subject from background, a background light controls the backdrop alone. Ratios — 2:1 gentle to 8:1 severe — are the taste dial. Build one light at a time, name each job, and keep the portrait you prefer, not the one with the most lights.
lessons.practice_brief: Field and equipment drill: build the four-stage setup — key only, key plus fill, plus rim, plus background — photographing at each stage and writing one line about what the light contributed. The classic patterns (Rembrandt, loop, butterfly, split) are key positions; verify each against the shadow shape you actually produced.

lessons.title: Advanced Composition and Visual Storytelling
lessons.summary: Composition carries meaning at the advanced level: gesture tells stories in bodies, color in mood, relationships in the frame. One subject can carry several stories, told by viewpoint and layering — and a sequence of images forms a sentence whose meaning changes with order. Compose for the story, then edit the story into a sequence.
lessons.practice_brief: Photograph one subject several ways to tell different stories, add the frames to your gallery, and sequence the strongest three in the workspace — reorder once and note the meaning shift. Load a picture style to hold the mood consistent across the set, and let the coach's reads show which frames carry the story hardest.

lessons.title: Specialist Genres
lessons.summary: Skills are shared; genres specialize by priority order. Wildlife demands shutter and patience, sports anticipation, architecture verticals, macro depth discipline, events consistency, food color honesty. The transfer method: take the skills you own, reorder the priorities for the genre's demands, and go deep on one — the others borrow.
lessons.practice_brief: The style selector IS this lesson: load Wildlife, Sports, Food, and Night styles in turn and watch each load a different priority order — shutter floors, ISO ceilings, aperture targets. Choose one genre, write its priority order, shoot one session in it, and review against the genre's demands rather than your general standards. Wildlife ethics hold everywhere: the animal's welfare outranks the photograph.

lessons.title: Long Exposure and Night Photography
lessons.summary: At night the rules reverse: the tripod is the exposure, focus happens once deliberately on a magnified live view, and metering gives way to test frames scaled into final exposures. Moving lights paint with time — thirty seconds of traffic becomes ribbons. Accept the noise the image earns, keep ISO as low as the shutter allows, and stop when the frames are considered.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator shows the trade you'll live at night: walk the shutter ladder from 1/8 toward seconds and watch brightness rise while the shake floor falls away — the reason the tripod is the exposure. Then the real drill: a tripod night scene, focused once deliberately, test frame at high ISO, scaled to the final exposure. Record test values and final values and the stops between.

lessons.title: Panorama, Focus Stacking, and HDR
lessons.summary: Three limits, three combinations. Framing wider than any lens: panorama. Depth beyond any aperture: focus stacking. Brightness beyond one frame: HDR. All three demand aligned captures — locked camera, consistent settings, generous overlap, one variable changed — and all three are rescues for real limits, not replacements for craft. The best photograph is still sometimes one frame.
lessons.practice_brief: Capture drill: choose the technique that solves a limit you actually hit — a wide panorama with 30% overlap, a close focus stack in even steps, or a two-stop HDR bracket. Combine in software and review honestly for seams, ghosts, and halos. Use the coach on the single frame first to confirm the limit was real before spending the extra captures.

lessons.title: Color Management and Print Preparation
lessons.summary: Screens emit light; paper reflects it — print is a translation. Color spaces are boxes, and delivery means the destination's box. Soft proofing rehearses the print so surprises become decisions; export at print size as a separate copy. The two rules that matter: proof first, original untouched.
lessons.practice_brief: The app's role is pre-judgment: analyze the file in the coach and confirm the histogram holds no clipping before it meets paper — and the gallery original stays untouched through every export, exactly as the workflow lesson demands. The soft proofing, export, and physical comparison happen in your editor and print service; note what the proof predicted and what it missed.

lessons.title: Advanced Retouching and Image Finishing
lessons.summary: Finishing is surgical: local light where the story needs it, accidents subtracted, targeted color shaping the eye's path. The lines are believable and honest — subtract the accidental, not the factual, and label what AI tools invent. The final test is the thumbnail: a finish that announces itself is a finish too far.
lessons.practice_brief: The simulator's controls are the restrained finish preview: EV for the local-brightness instinct, white balance and picture style for the color path — each move small, each answering 'does this serve the photograph?' Then the surgical layer happens in your editor: dodge, burn, subtract the accidental. Finish with the thumbnail test — small view, beside the original.

lessons.title: Image Selection and Sequencing
lessons.summary: The edit is where photographers are made. First pass ruthless and fast — the technically dead go without sentiment. Second pass judged against stated criteria, not mood. Order is meaning: the opening sets, middles develop with varied rhythm, the closing lands. Darlings that break the sequence's rhythm go to a folder of their own.
lessons.practice_brief: The gallery and Progress screen are the editing table: take this week's gallery set, cut the technically dead, judge survivors against stated criteria, and sequence the survivors into a story with a deliberate opening and closing. Load each finalist into the coach — its read is one vote, not the verdict. Write the one-sentence story and verify the sequence tells it.

lessons.title: Developing a Personal Style
lessons.summary: Style is found, then chosen. Audit thirty of your own images across four columns — light, color, subject, composition — and name the patterns you never planned. Keep the loved patterns as commitments; practice at the edges you avoid. Borrow technique freely — the voice comes from your own frames, and the fastest route to a generic portfolio is a borrowed style.
lessons.practice_brief: The Progress screen is the audit table: your saved analyses carry scores, styles, and history across shoots. Read them for patterns — which light scores best, which style recurs, what subject keeps returning. Name three patterns (at least one unplanned), write three commitments for the next shoot, and one edge you'll practice. Shoot for the commitments; audit again after.

lessons.title: Ethics, Permission, and Responsible Photography
lessons.summary: Advanced skills carry advanced responsibilities. Consent precedes the shutter when people are involved — and publication consent is separate. Selection is a claim: hold it fairly. Editing stays believable and honest, captions included, and AI-assisted inventions are owned. Write your positions down — deliberate responsibility is the advanced photographer's real signature.
lessons.practice_brief: Take three of your own photographs and write the ethical review of each: who appears and did they meaningfully consent to photo AND publication, what the frame claims, what was edited, and whether you'd defend it publicly. The app keeps those photos private to your device — a safe place to practice the judgment before the public ever sees a frame.

courses.title: Pro Photography Class
courses.tagline: The business of photography — the complete 12-lesson class
courses.description: The class that turns craft into a practice, in twelve lessons: finding a professional niche (1), client consultation and briefs (2), pricing and estimates (3), contracts, licensing and usage rights (4), professional shoot planning (5), managing a commercial shoot (6), professional file and backup management (7), client proofing and delivery (8), portfolio and website development (9), marketing and business operations (10), working with assistants and creative teams (11), and professional standards and risk management (12). Legal and insurance specifics are pointed to qualified professionals — this class teaches the vocabulary, the structure, and the habits.

lessons.title: Finding a Professional Niche
lessons.summary: You can photograph anything and still need to be known for something. A niche lives where four inputs overlap: interests (what you shoot unpaid), strengths (what your best images share), clients (a market, not one buyer), and working style (the conditions you can sustain). Write the overlap as one sentence, test it against five real client names, and narrow first — widen later.
lessons.practice_brief: The app supplies the evidence for the audit: your Progress screen history and the Advanced style-audit method reveal which subjects and lights you already gravitate toward — and the style selector shows which genres you've practiced. Write the niche sentence from those four inputs, then pressure-test it: list five real potential clients. Five names won't come? Revise the niche toward the names that do.

lessons.title: Client Consultation and Briefs
lessons.summary: An inquiry that starts with 'how much for photos?' must grow into a brief before it becomes a quote. Five questions: goal (what is the photo for), audience (who sees it), deliverables (count, formats, sizes), schedule (dates that are fixed), expectations (locations, style, who approves). Listen for the unsaid, write the brief back in the client's vocabulary, and update it in writing when scope moves.
lessons.practice_brief: Written-work drill: take a real or invented five-line inquiry and conduct the five-question consultation in writing — in the client's vocabulary. Produce the one-page brief, send it to a friend playing the client, and let them misunderstand one line. Correcting it in writing IS the lesson. Use the coach on any reference images the client shares to learn the look they mean.

lessons.title: Pricing and Estimates
lessons.summary: Price the iceberg: preparation, shooting, editing, administration — a half-day shoot is routinely a three-day project. License what the image will DO (who, where, how long, exclusive) — clients buy uses, not photographs. Add project expenses and profit, which is not a wage. Present itemized with payment terms and an expiry, so scope changes show which line moves. All example numbers in the lesson are examples, not rates.
lessons.practice_brief: Build two estimates: the bakery brief from Lesson 2 with your own rate and hours — consultation, scouting, shoot, editing, admin, license, expenses, margin — and a second brief of your invention. Compare which line surprised you. Then write down the line you were tempted to hide; that's usually the one clients most deserve to see.

lessons.title: Contracts, Licensing, and Usage Rights
lessons.summary: The agreement anchors five things to the brief: scope, payment, usage rights, responsibilities, and resolution — protecting both sides. Usage rights have four dimensions: who uses, where, how long, and exclusively. Walk every agreement from both seats, mark what's unclear, and raise legal specifics with a qualified professional in your jurisdiction. When the client sends THEIR paper, read the license clause first. This lesson teaches vocabulary and questions — it is not legal advice.
lessons.practice_brief: Walk the sample agreement twice: once as the photographer (what's protected, what's missing), once as the client (what's unclear in plain language). Write the two questions you'd take to a qualified professional and the two clarifications you'd request from the client. Compare lists with a working photographer if you know one.

lessons.title: Professional Shoot Planning
lessons.summary: Planning is shooting that happens early. Extract the shoot from the approved brief: a shot list (one line per deliverable group — the list is a floor, not a cage), a schedule worked backwards from light and availability, a location plan (positions, light direction, gear staging), an equipment list pulled shot by shot, and one written contingency per likely failure. Shoot day's job becomes execution.
lessons.practice_brief: Build the full pre-shoot checklist for a real or invented brief — shot list, backwards schedule, location map, equipment pulled line by line, contingencies written. Scout with the app: test frames at the location analyzed in the coach tell you the light's direction and the histogram's shape before shoot day. Hand the checklist to someone and ask them to break it.

lessons.title: Managing a Commercial Shoot
lessons.summary: The checklist meets the day. Brief everyone: list order, schedule anchors, one role each. Work the list in order — bonus frames welcome, always return. Manage the client in real time: show frames, translate ideas into the list, surface trade-offs with the timeline in hand. When it goes sideways, adapt aloud with pre-decided contingencies. Close with the wrap habit: list verified, gear counted, next step promised.
lessons.practice_brief: Run one shoot from your Lesson 5 checklist at any scale, including one deliberate adaptation and the wrap habit. Use the coach on set between setups — a quick read catches exposure drift before the client notices. Write down what went sideways and which pre-decided contingency caught it.

lessons.title: Professional File and Backup Management
lessons.summary: Professionals are judged by what they don't lose. Card discipline: import first, verify counts and spot-checks, and never format until delivery. Working structure that scales: dated, client-coded, originals untouched, exports separated. Backups by 3-2-1 — three copies, two media, one off-site — on a schedule and test-restored. Versioning by structure and date: 'final_final_v2' is the sound of a system that doesn't exist.
lessons.practice_brief: Run one shoot's files through the professional path: import, verify, working structure, 3-2-1 backup, test-restore. The app's gallery originals are the model — untouched originals, working previews beside them, everything findable in one minute. Time the whole path; simplify anything too cumbersome to repeat, because a workflow you skip is the one that fails.

lessons.title: Client Proofing and Delivery
lessons.summary: Delivery is part of the product. Proof edited-enough candidates — your strongest, ordered — with written selection rules and a deadline (the deadline is a kindness). Deliver exactly what the brief and license define: folders that name themselves, sizes as agreed, the license summary in writing, and a handoff note. Close the project folder with complete records — the next project's head start.
lessons.practice_brief: Run one delivery end to end: proof a set with written rules, gather selections against a deadline, handle over-selection using the estimate's scope line, deliver folders that name themselves with the license summary, and close the project folder — brief, estimate, agreement, proofs, selections, delivered files, all findable in one minute.

lessons.title: Portfolio and Website Development
lessons.summary: A portfolio is an argument for a specific job — not an archive of your best work. Choose the audience first; prove the niche with depth, currency, and range; win the first five images with consistent crops and editing; and verify the site minimums: the niche sentence where a stranger lands, an about page with a real photo, a working contact path, mobile layout. Two audiences means two arguments.
lessons.practice_brief: Build or refresh a portfolio for ONE audience: select against the niche's promise using the Advanced selection passes, order for the first five images, and verify the five website minimums. Use the coach's scores across your gallery to find the strongest candidates objectively. Then show it to someone in the target audience and ask what they'd hire you for — their answer grades the argument.

lessons.title: Marketing and Business Operations
lessons.summary: Operations are the quiet half. Every project walks the same ten-stage map — inquiry, consultation, brief, estimate, agreement, planning, shoot, selection, delivery, follow-up — with a template at each stage. Promotion is steady presence: portfolio current, niche channels fed, referrals asked at delivery (the moment of maximum goodwill). The tracking board holds the truth: pending, owed, needs-a-nudge. An hour a week keeps the pipeline alive.
lessons.practice_brief: Draw your inquiry-to-delivery map with the templates you own, build the tracking board (a column per stage, a card per inquiry), and run one real or simulated inquiry through every stage — updating the board each time. Book the between-shoots hour: portfolio refresh, one outreach, board updated. The Progress screen doubles as your work-quality tracker across engagements.

lessons.title: Working with Assistants and Creative Teams
lessons.summary: Growing past one pair of hands. Every helper gets a name and a job: assistant, second shooter, stylist, coordinator — ownership, not enthusiasm. One page and five minutes of briefing prevent on-set guessing. On set: quiet, clear, repeated — requests by name, transitions announced to everyone. Close the loop with specific, prompt feedback. The same habits that run clients run teams.
lessons.practice_brief: Run one shoot with at least one helper: write the one-page team brief, hold the five-minute meeting (each person says their job aloud), use named requests and announced transitions on set, and close with specific feedback including one thing they did better than expected. Write down what you'd brief differently next time.

lessons.title: Professional Standards and Risk Management
lessons.summary: The professional's last habit: walk every planned shoot through five risk categories — people (safety outranks photographs), places (permissions verified in writing), equipment (failure points and backups), data (the card discipline applies), reputation (what could this shoot do to your name). One written contingency line per category, and the written positions document — ethics plus risk — becomes the practice's constitution. Insurance questions go to qualified professionals, not videos.
lessons.practice_brief: Take a planned shoot through the five-category risk walk in writing: people, places, equipment, data, reputation — one contingency line each. Update the written positions document from the Advanced ethics lesson with the risk habits. In the app, review the ethics positions against real photos: who appears, what the frame claims, would you defend it publicly — the same judgment, now at professional scale.

courses.title: Shoot the Moon
courses.tagline: The easiest night subject that everyone gets wrong
courses.description: A four-lesson romp through moon photography: why the auto modes blow the moon into a white blob (it's a sunlit rock!), phases and moonrise planning, reach and detail, and putting the moon into a landscape. Fun, practical, and the first night subject anyone can nail.

lessons.title: The moon is a sunlit rock
lessons.summary: The moon isn't a night scene — it's a rock lit by full daylight, which is why auto modes blow it into a white blob. Expose for the rock: roughly f/8, 1/250, ISO 200 for a full moon, and read the histogram of the disc itself. If it touches the right wall, the texture is gone.
lessons.practice_brief: The reframe drill: expose a night scene normally and watch the moon-shaped highlight clip in the histogram — the auto modes' mistake, visible. Then pull −EV until the disc holds texture: f/8, 1/250, ISO 200 is the starting card. The moon follows the daylight-exposure rules you already know.

lessons.title: Phases and planning
lessons.summary: The moon rises about an hour later each day, and its phase changes everything: a full moon rises at sunset with flat, front-lit light; crescents rise near the sun with raking light that carves craters along the terminator. Moon apps predict phase, rise time, and position — plan like the Advanced class taught.
lessons.practice_brief: Phase drill: expose the crescent mood — the dark side needs ISO and wider aperture to show earthshine, while the lit crescent edge needs discipline. Two moons, two exposures, one simulator: walk both exposure cards and watch the terminator detail appear.

lessons.title: Reach and detail
lessons.summary: The moon fills the frame only through serious reach — 600mm effective and up. But detail comes from discipline, not reach alone: tripod, manual focus on the terminator using live-view magnification, and the f/8–f/11 range where most lenses are sharpest. Cropping with intent completes what reach starts.
lessons.practice_brief: Reach drill with the lens selector: mount the longest lens in the list and watch the swap badge grow the moon. Then the sharpness walk: f/5.6, f/8, f/11 on the same disc, enlarged — find where your lens peaks. Manual focus on the terminator edge, live view magnified.

lessons.title: The moon in the landscape
lessons.summary: Put the moon in a scene and the two-brightness problem appears: expose for the landscape and the moon becomes a blown blob; expose for the moon and the land goes black. Decide early — silhouette composition, or bracket for blending the Advanced exposure way. Moon apps predict where it rises against your landmarks.
lessons.practice_brief: The two-brightness drill: expose for the landscape and watch the disc clip; expose for the disc and watch the land die. Both are legitimate frames — decide which one you're making. Then the position bonus: moon apps show where it rises against your landmark, and the simulator's EV walk rehearses the compromise.

lessons.title: Beyond the full moon
lessons.summary: The moon's moods: crescent slivers need longer exposures and show earthshine on the dark side; eclipses turn copper and need a stop or two more than the full moon; moonbows exist for the devoted. Build your exposure cards per phase — then the next full moon is a planned shot, not a lucky one.
lessons.practice_brief: The card drill: build your exposure cards — full moon, crescent, eclipse — as one-page plans per phase. Then the assignment: shoot the next full moon with the plan, and one crescent within the week. The app's coach reviews both; the moon keeps its secrets for nobody who planned.

courses.title: Following the Rainbow
courses.tagline: The weather-reader's party trick — find it, expose it, compose it
courses.description: A four-lesson game of anticipation: the geometry that makes rainbows appear (sun behind, rain ahead), the exposure trick that keeps the arc vivid, composition that gives the sky-filling guest a subject, and the weather-reader's habit that finds them before other people do.

lessons.title: Chasing the geometry
lessons.summary: Rainbows obey geometry, not luck: the sun must be BEHIND you and the rain in front, with the sun low in the sky. When you see one, turn your back to the sun first — then compose. The arc's center is always the shadow of your own head.
lessons.practice_brief: Geometry drill, in the field after rain with breaking sun: turn your back to the sun first, find the arc, and photograph it. Note the sun's height — low sun means a taller arc. No rainbow today? The simulator can't fake one, but the landscape style readies the scene for when the sky cooperates.

lessons.title: Exposure and the dim arc
lessons.summary: The arc is one to two stops dimmer than the sky around it — so the meter's guess washes it out. Underexpose slightly to saturate it, and remove your polarizer (polarizers dim rainbows, the opposite of every other sky effect). A darker background sky makes the same arc more vivid.
lessons.practice_brief: The exposure trick in the simulator: darken the frame one stop with EV and watch a dim band gain saturation — the rainbow's advantage is contrast against a darkened sky. Then the field version: shoot the next arc at 0 and −1 EV and compare which holds the colors.

lessons.title: Composition with a sky-filling guest
lessons.summary: The rainbow is huge — so give it a subject. Wide to include the full semicircle, or tight on where it touches down; a tree, a road, a person under the arc turns a weather event into a photograph. And when the fainter second rainbow appears, decide: both, or isolate the bright one.
lessons.practice_brief: Composition drill: the arc alone is a snapshot. Wide frame with a foreground anchor under the arc, then a tight frame where it touches the ground — two photographs, two stories. Spot the secondary bow and decide deliberately: include the pair or isolate the star.

lessons.title: The weather-reader's habit
lessons.summary: Rainbows can't be scheduled — only anticipated. Sun low behind you plus rain ahead equals look up: weather apps show the rain-then-clear pattern, and the Landscape style readies the scene. The habit is the class: every time rain falls with sun on your back, check the sky. The rainbow finds the prepared.
lessons.practice_brief: The habit drill, written: your rainbow checklist — sun behind you, rain ahead, polarizer off, −1 EV, subject under the arc — taped to the camera bag. Then the commitment: for one week, every time rain falls with sun on your back, look up and shoot what's there. Load the Landscape style for the scene; the arc hangs it in the frame.

courses.title: Northern Lights
courses.tagline: The hunt: forecast, freeze, and foreground
courses.description: Four lessons on the aurora hunt: the forecast deal (latitude, Kp index, apps), the all-manual camera setup, exposing a light that dances, and foregrounds that turn a weather event into a photograph — with cold-weather honesty about batteries and patience. Certified night-photography skills from the Advanced class assumed.

lessons.title: The aurora deal: latitude, Kp, and apps
lessons.summary: The aurora is forecast, not scheduled: high latitude, dark skies, clear weather, and geomagnetic activity (the Kp index) must all agree. Apps predict hours ahead — plan a window of nights, not a night. Manage expectations honestly: the hunt is the reward, the lights are the bonus.
lessons.practice_brief: The hunt-plan drill, written: location, date window, backup nights, the forecast apps you'll check, and the bail-out criteria. Load the Astrophotography style — its wide-open, high-ISO recipe is the aurora's starting point. The plan is the lesson: the lights refuse schedules.

lessons.title: The camera setup: manual everything
lessons.summary: Aurora setup is manual everything: focus to infinity on a star or distant light with live view magnification, lens wide open, RAW, tripod locked, delayed shutter. The exposure balance is ISO 1600–3200, f/2.8, 2–15 seconds — fast enough to hold the curtain's shape, slow enough to gather it.
lessons.practice_brief: Setup drill in the simulator: manual focus imagined on infinity, then the exposure walk — ISO 3200, f/2.8, and shutter from 15s down to 2s. Watch the star smear begin as seconds stretch: the shutter ceiling is where the curtain's shape survives. That ceiling is your frame.

lessons.title: Exposing the dance
lessons.summary: The aurora dances: fast curtains want 2–5 second exposures, slow glows tolerate 15. The histogram rule holds in the cold — pull the data off the left wall without clipping the brightest green. Bright displays tolerate lower ISO; faint ones demand everything the sensor has.
lessons.practice_brief: Exposure drill: the night lesson's test-driven method, colder. Test frame at high ISO, read the histogram, scale down and stretch the shutter. In the simulator: walk ISO and shutter at f/2.8 until the shape clears the left wall — the exact decisions you'll make at minus ten.

lessons.title: Foregrounds: the aurora needs a subject
lessons.summary: An aurora-only frame is a weather photo. The lights are the sky; the PHOTOGRAPH is the place — a cabin, trees, a frozen lake's reflection. Scout the foreground in daylight per the Advanced planning habit, so the night frame composes itself when the sky finally performs.
lessons.practice_brief: Composition drill: three foreground choices for one sky — a cabin silhouette, treeline, and a still-lake reflection — scouted in daylight and marked. When the lights arrive, the frame is already composed: sky does the performing, foreground does the storytelling.

lessons.title: Cold, batteries, and the hunt
lessons.summary: Cold kills batteries — spares live in an inside pocket, not the bag. No lens changes in the field; the sealed-bag return indoors defeats condensation. And the final Pro-class habit: three nights committed beats one hopeful evening — the hunt is the reward, and the night-photography skill is the prize.
lessons.practice_brief: The cold drill, written: your cold-night kit — spare batteries in the inside pocket, no lens changes outside, bag-sealed return indoors, hand warmers for the tripod's joints. Then the commitment: a three-night window in your hunt plan, with the foregrounds scouted in daylight. The aurora finds the prepared.

courses.title: Mastering the Exposure Triangle
courses.tagline: Read the subject, pick the priority, blend the triangle
courses.description: The class every photographer wishes they'd had first. Seven short lessons build exposure from the ground up: what exposure actually is, the three settings that control it, and the priority-first habit professionals use — identify the subject first, choose the one non-negotiable setting, and blend the other two around it. Every lesson ends in the live simulator so you feel each trade instead of memorizing it.

lessons.title: What is exposure?
lessons.summary: Exposure is the total amount of light your sensor records while the shutter is open. Too little and shadows turn muddy, then black; too much and highlights wash out to white with no texture. The whole game is landing the light between those walls — and everything else in this course is just three dials that control that one number.
lessons.practice_brief: Tap exposure compensation +1 EV, then −1 EV, and watch the histogram slide toward each wall. Clipping at the edges means detail is gone forever. Want to go deeper? Click the histogram itself for the guided tour.

lessons.title: Meet the three settings
lessons.summary: Three dials, three ways to control the same light. Shutter speed sets how LONG light is collected — a time door. Aperture sets how WIDE the light funnel opens — a size door. ISO sets how SENSITIVE the sensor is to whatever it collects. Each one brightens or darkens the photo, and each drags a side effect: shutter brings motion blur, aperture brings depth of field, ISO brings grain. Memorize the side effects — they, not brightness, decide which dial you reach for first.
lessons.practice_brief: Brighten this photo three different ways: slow the shutter, open the aperture, raise the ISO. Same brightness each time — but watch what changes besides brightness. Name the side effect out loud; that habit is the whole course.

lessons.title: Blend them: three dials, one brightness
lessons.summary: Each full stop doubles or halves the light. Open the aperture one stop and you can shoot the shutter twice as fast at the same brightness — the light you gave up on one dial, you take back on another. That swapping is the triangle: brightness stays constant while you trade side effects. Master the swap and no scene can trap you.
lessons.practice_brief: You start at f/16 and 1/30 — deep depth of field but handheld shake territory. Open two stops to f/8 (light ×4) and speed the shutter two stops to 1/125 (light ÷4). Same brightness, no shake, thinner depth. You just blended the triangle.

lessons.title: Pick your priority first
lessons.summary: Exposure is three unknowns, so decide which ONE is non-negotiable before you touch anything. First identify what you are photographing — the subject picks the priority. A moving subject makes shutter speed the priority: choose it first and let the other two follow. A subject you want lifted from the background makes aperture the priority. Dim handheld light makes the shake floor the constraint and ISO fills the gap. One dial gets picked first; the other two are bookkeeping.
lessons.practice_brief: This is a running dog at 1/30 — motion smear everywhere. Shutter is the priority, so snap it to 1/250 or faster FIRST. Only then fix the brightness with aperture, and let ISO absorb whatever is left.

lessons.title: Shutter speed: a slice of time
lessons.summary: Every photo of a moving subject is a slice of time. The faster the subject moves, the thinner the slice you need to stop the action and capture the moment: 1/1000 freezes a bird in flight, 1/250 holds a runner, 1/60 captures a stroll. Below about 1/60 your own hands join the motion — that is the shake floor, and image stabilization buys you roughly four stops below it. Want blur on purpose, like silk waterfalls or light trails? Take a thick slice.
lessons.practice_brief: Walk the shutter from 1/30 up to 1/1000 and watch the motion smear shrink with every step — you are thinning the slice of time. Find the stop where your subject would freeze, then notice what the darkening did and how you would pay it back.

lessons.title: Aperture: the depth dial
lessons.summary: Aperture does two jobs at once. The light job: how wide the funnel opens. The story job: depth of field — the zone of sharpness around your focus point. Change the aperture and you move that zone: wide open gives a thin zone, so eyes are sharp while the background melts away; stopped down gives a deep zone, sharp from foreground to horizon. Here is the trap beginners miss: perfect focus does not mean sharp — a subject outside the depth of field lands soft no matter how precisely you focused. The focus point picks WHERE the zone sits; aperture picks how THICK it is. And the numbering runs backwards: f-stops count how far the aperture is CLOSED, not how big the hole is — f/2 is barely closed (big hole, lots of light, fast), f/16 is nearly shut (a pinhole). That is why the smaller f-number lets more light in, faster.
lessons.practice_brief: Step the aperture from f/16 to the widest stop and watch two things move together: background blur grows AND the image brightens. Now pay the light back with the shutter and watch brightness return while the blur stays — that is the depth dial working separately from exposure.

lessons.title: ISO: sensitivity, then and now
lessons.summary: ISO is how sensitive to light your camera is set. In the film days that sensitivity lived in the chemistry of the film itself — you chose it when you bought the roll, and the whole roll lived with the decision. Digital flipped it: each frame gets its own choice, made by amplifying the sensor's signal. The cost of amplification is grain. So treat ISO as the flex knob: lock your priority dial and your story dial first, then let ISO absorb whatever light is left — keeping it as low as the scene allows.
lessons.practice_brief: Start at ISO 6400 and step down toward 100, paying the brightness back with shutter or aperture as you go. Watch the grain fade at every step — that ladder is your camera's real noise budget. Finish by clicking the histogram to see how the whole session reshaped it.

courses.title: Introduction to Digital Photography
courses.tagline: Exposure, composition and lighting — the foundations
courses.description: The complete starting point: what exposure really is, how to compose a frame that holds attention, and how to see light like a photographer. Every lesson ends with a hands-on drill in the simulator.

lessons.title: What exposure really means
lessons.summary: Exposure is how much light hits the sensor — controlled by the triangle of aperture, shutter speed and ISO. This lesson builds the mental model: three knobs, one brightness, three different side effects.
lessons.practice_brief: Start balanced. Now slow the shutter one stop and watch the preview brighten — then raise ISO one stop to bring it back. Same brightness, different side effects. That's the whole triangle.

lessons.title: Composition: giving the eye a path
lessons.summary: Rule of thirds, leading lines, clean edges and subject separation. Composition is arranging the frame so the viewer looks where you want — here's the vocabulary and the drills.
lessons.practice_brief: Framing is yours to make — but notice how the depth-of-field blur (open the aperture wider) can isolate a subject and clean a cluttered background for you.

lessons.title: Seeing light: direction, quality, color
lessons.summary: Hard vs soft light, front vs side vs back lighting, and the color of different light sources. The subject of every photo is really the light falling on it.
lessons.practice_brief: Indoor bulbs are orange and dim — this preset mimics that struggle. Try the Tungsten white balance preset and watch the cast vanish.

lessons.title: Holding and moving the camera
lessons.summary: Stance, elbows, breathing and the shutter press — plus when to raise ISO instead of dropping below your handheld shutter floor.
lessons.practice_brief: 1/15s handheld is asking for blur. Step the shutter up until the smear disappears — that's your personal handheld floor, and it's why ISO exists.

courses.title: Motion, Blur & Freeze
courses.tagline: Make blur a choice, not an accident
courses.description: Shutter speed decides whether motion is frozen, hinted, or smeared into streaks. Two lessons: freezing action cleanly, then using slow shutters deliberately — including the pan that pros use.

lessons.title: Where freeze ends
lessons.summary: Every subject has a shutter threshold where blur begins. Find yours with the smear simulator, then keep a safety margin for the ones that matter.
lessons.practice_brief: Walk the shutter from 1/60 down to 1" and back. Notice the smear kicks in below about 1/60 — that's the handheld shake floor, and it's also the motion line for walking subjects.

lessons.title: Deliberate blur: the pan
lessons.summary: Panning — moving the camera with the subject — keeps the subject readable while the world streaks. It's a wrist skill, and this lesson drills the timing.
lessons.practice_brief: 1/15s is pan territory. In the field: track the subject through the shot and keep moving after the shutter fires. Expect 1 keeper in 20 at first — it's a wrist skill.

courses.title: Photography Masterclass
courses.tagline: Basic to advanced — the complete journey
courses.description: A comprehensive course that includes both basic and advanced techniques: mastering light in every condition, advanced composition, color theory, and the workflows that tie it all together. The graduation course after the fundamentals.

lessons.title: Advanced exposure: histograms and ETTR
lessons.summary: Reading the histogram like a pro, exposing to the right (ETTR) for maximum quality, and when to deliberately break the rules.
lessons.practice_brief: Watch the histogram as you push exposure comp up — the goal is riding the right edge without spilling over. That's ETTR: maximum data, minimum noise.

lessons.title: Light mastery: golden hour to blue hour
lessons.summary: Why photographers chase sunrise and sunset, how to expose when the light is dying, and white balance as a creative tool rather than a correctness chore.
lessons.practice_brief: Golden hour light is warm and low. Try WB Shade on a daylight scene — the deliberate warmth is a style choice, not an error.

lessons.title: Composition II: breaking the grid
lessons.summary: Beyond thirds: frames within frames, negative space as a subject, reflection and symmetry, and knowing when center composition wins.
lessons.practice_brief: f/8 keeps everything sharp — now the composition carries the whole frame. Rehearse three different arrangements of the same scene.

lessons.title: Color theory for photographers
lessons.summary: Complementary and analogous color, using color contrast to guide the eye, and Picture Styles / Creative Looks as a starting palette.
lessons.practice_brief: Cycle the Picture Styles on one frame — Vivid vs Neutral vs Monochrome changes the story before any editing.

lessons.title: Focusing systems in depth
lessons.summary: AF modes, AF-area choices, back-button focus and trap focusing — take full manual control of where and when the camera focuses.
lessons.practice_brief: Switch to AF-C and imagine tracking a runner: continuous focus plus a fast shutter is the sports combo. The Focus point dot shows where the sharp zone sits.

lessons.title: The photographer's workflow
lessons.summary: From pre-visualization to culling, editing and delivery — how pros move from idea to finished image without drowning in files.
lessons.practice_brief: Recreate your best-ever shot from memory using only the simulator — settings, framing intent, light. If you can rebuild it, you understood it.

courses.title: Portrait Photography
courses.tagline: Light, connection and flattering technique
courses.description: Techniques for capturing compelling portraits: shaping light on a face, directing people naturally, choosing backgrounds that flatter, and the settings that keep eyes sharp.

lessons.title: Flattering light: window, shade and golden hour
lessons.summary: Soft light flatters skin; hard light sculpts it. Where to place your subject relative to a window or the sun, and why overcast is a portrait photographer's friend.
lessons.practice_brief: Portrait starting point: wide open at f/2, 1/200s. Watch the background melt — then drag the focus dot onto the face to see the sharp zone you must protect.

lessons.title: The eyes have it: focus and connection
lessons.summary: Single-point AF on the near eye, aperture choices for one person vs groups, and how eye contact changes the whole image.
lessons.practice_brief: f/2 on a portrait lens is razor-thin. Open the aperture stepper wider and watch the focus zone shrink — the eyes survive, the ears don't.

lessons.title: Backgrounds that flatter
lessons.summary: Distance, tone and clutter: how to choose and control what's behind your subject, in camera, before you shoot.
lessons.practice_brief: Same subject, messy background? Wider aperture plus more subject-to-background distance is the recipe — the simulator shows the blur difference instantly.

lessons.title: Directing people who hate photos
lessons.summary: Prompts instead of poses, movement exercises, shooting during the in-between moments, and camera confidence that transfers to the subject.
lessons.practice_brief: Candid frames need faster shutters for laughter-in-motion: 1/320s and burst mode. The best expression often lives between the poses.

courses.title: Street Photography
courses.tagline: Candid moments in public spaces
courses.description: How to photograph people and scenes in public spaces: pre-setting your camera, reading light in the city, working a scene patiently, and the ethics of candid photography.

lessons.title: Pre-set and wait: the street method
lessons.summary: Set exposure for the light, pre-focus a zone, and let the scene come to you. The street classic — camera ready before the moment exists.
lessons.practice_brief: f/5.6 at 3m gives a deep-enough zone for walking subjects. Load it, then practice being ready — the drill is patience, not settings.

lessons.title: City light: reflections, shadows and rain
lessons.summary: Urban light is dramatic: hard sun through buildings, glowing shop signs, wet pavement mirrors. Learn to hunt light, not subjects.
lessons.practice_brief: Shadows and highlights are the composition. Expose for the bright lane and let the rest go dark — underexposing on purpose is a street superpower.

lessons.title: Ethics, nerve and the candid frame
lessons.summary: When to raise the camera, how to handle being noticed, and the respect that keeps street photography welcome in public spaces.
lessons.practice_brief: Evening streets push ISO up — this preset accepts the grain to keep a safe shutter. Grain is the honest cost of being there.

courses.title: Fine Art Photography
courses.tagline: Storytelling and meaningful images
courses.description: Emphasizes storytelling and creating meaningful images: developing a personal vision, using long exposure and minimalism deliberately, and building a body of work that says something.

lessons.title: Vision before settings
lessons.summary: What do you want the viewer to feel? Turning an emotion into exposure, tone and framing choices — 'wrong' settings on purpose.
lessons.practice_brief: The long exposure turns anything moving into smoke — motion becomes the story. Darkness is a mood, not a mistake.

lessons.title: Minimalism: subject, space, silence
lessons.summary: Removing until only meaning remains. Negative space, isolation, and the discipline of leaving things out.
lessons.practice_brief: Sharp subject, vast emptiness. Frame a small subject with huge negative space using the composition you imagined — the settings are deliberately boring.

lessons.title: Building a series
lessons.summary: One image is a moment; twelve images are a statement. Consistency in tone, treatment and subject — and sequencing that builds meaning.
lessons.practice_brief: Series work demands repeatable settings. Lock this recipe, then go make variations — consistency is the craft here.

courses.title: Night & Celestial Photography
courses.tagline: Stars, cityscapes and long exposures after dark
courses.description: The full night class: tripods, the 500 rule, star fields, cityscapes and light pollution. Five lessons take you from your first blurry attempt to pin-point stars and glowing skylines.

lessons.title: Why night is a tripod problem
lessons.summary: Night exposures need seconds, not fractions. What changes when the shutter is open for 10s: technique, stability, and how you think about ISO.
lessons.practice_brief: Load the night starting point. Try handheld-style shutters (1/30) and watch the underexposure — then commit to the 8s exposure and see where the light comes from.

lessons.title: The 500 rule
lessons.summary: Stars smear because the Earth turns. The 500 rule gives the longest shutter that keeps stars as points for your focal length — here's the math made visual.
lessons.practice_brief: At 24mm your limit is about 20s. Compare 10s vs 20s vs 30s exposures and watch brightness climb while trailing threatens — that trade is the whole lesson.

lessons.title: Cityscapes: tame the lights
lessons.summary: City lights are your subject and your hazard. Exposure strategy for skylines that glow without clipping, plus white balance for mixed sodium/LED light.
lessons.practice_brief: f/8 at 4s keeps buildings crisp while lights accumulate. Watch the histogram's right edge as you lengthen the shutter — stop before it stacks against the wall.

lessons.title: Noise strategy after dark
lessons.summary: High ISO is unavoidable at night — the skill is knowing how far to push and how to recover. ISO invariants, exposure-to-noise ratio, and when to accept grain.
lessons.practice_brief: Same brightness, two routes: ISO 6400 at 2" versus ISO 1600 at 8". Compare the grain — that difference is why tripods exist.

lessons.title: Field checklist & drills
lessons.summary: The pre-dark checklist: batteries, focus at infinity, live histogram habits — and the four drills from this class turned into a repeatable practice plan.
lessons.practice_brief: Run the full night starting recipe, then verify each leg of the triangle against the checklist: aperture wide, shutter at the rule, ISO at your tested ceiling.

courses.title: Commercial Photography
courses.tagline: Advertising, product and marketing imagery
courses.description: Covers photography for advertising and marketing purposes: product shots on white, controlled studio lighting, working to a brief, and the precision commercial clients expect.

lessons.title: Product on white: the commercial baseline
lessons.summary: Even light, deep depth of field, exact exposure — product work is precision. Setting up a basic two-light white-background shot with any camera.
lessons.practice_brief: Commercial baseline: f/8 front-to-back sharpness at base ISO. Nothing artistic here — consistency IS the product.

lessons.title: Working to a brief
lessons.summary: Clients speak in adjectives ('clean', 'premium', 'bold'). Translating vague words into light, angle and composition decisions — and shooting for the edit.
lessons.practice_brief: Shoot the same product three ways — clean, premium, bold — by changing angle and light, not just adjectives. The simulator shows the exposure differences.

lessons.title: Lighting for advertising looks
lessons.summary: Soft boxes, gradients, rim light and reflections: the lighting patterns behind premium-looking commercial images, scaled down to a desk setup.
lessons.practice_brief: f/11 plus controlled light: every edge defined, every highlight intentional. This is where manual everything stops being optional.

lessons.title: E-commerce volume: consistency at scale
lessons.summary: Online stores need fifty products that look like ONE store: identical light, angle, and color across every frame. Build a repeatable set — locked tripod, fixed lights, a jig for placement — and shoot products like an assembly line, editing them to match. Consistency is the deliverable.
lessons.practice_brief: Volume drill: shoot five products of different sizes and colors on one locked set — identical framing, light, and exposure per product. Then compare the set: every product should sit at the same scale and color truth. The Commercial style's color-honesty priorities are the judge.

courses.title: Post-Processing Techniques
courses.tagline: Lightroom, Photoshop and the digital darkroom
courses.description: Focuses on editing photos using software like Photoshop and Lightroom: RAW workflow, exposure and color grading, retouching, and building an edit that serves the image instead of decorating it.

lessons.title: RAW workflow: why shoot RAW
lessons.summary: What a RAW file actually is, why it survives edits JPEGs can't, and the import → cull → develop → export loop in Lightroom.
lessons.practice_brief: Editing starts in camera: shoot RAW (check your camera's menu) and this lesson's recovery tricks become possible. The simulator's histogram is your preview of what RAW can fix.

lessons.title: Exposure and color grading in Lightroom
lessons.summary: The develop panel in order: exposure → contrast → white balance → HSL color → sharpening. A repeatable grading recipe that works on any photo.
